_comment: Measured infrastructure ceilings for the cross-framework comparison. The
driver reads this so the 70%-of-ceiling headroom rule is ENFORCED rather than
checked by hand — an arm above the limit is refused, not warned about.
Stored in MESSAGES per second, deliberately, not rows per second. The ceiling
is a property of the consume path, which moves messages; rows per second
depends on EVENTS_PER_BATCH. Storing rows would mean that changing the fan-out
silently invalidated this file, which is exactly the class of mistake that
produced several retracted numbers already. The driver multiplies by the
KAFKA_CPUS=8 PARTITIONS=8 PAYLOAD=840 MESSAGES=3000000 kafka_topology produce
KAFKA_CPUS=8 PARTITIONS=8 PAYLOAD=840 DURATION_S=8 MODE=split INSTANCES=1 \
DURATION_S must be short enough that the backlog outlasts the pass, or the rig

measured.shape: MODE=split INSTANCES=1 THREADS=4 — the shape etl-kafka itself uses
measured.host: Apple Silicon, Docker Desktop, 18 vCPU, arm64

notes: This is a single-process CLIENT ceiling, not the broker's serving limit.
Doubling the broker 4 -> 8 CPU moved it ~1% (302,334 -> 305,554 msgs/s split;
333,444 -> 337,694 perthread), and matching REDPANDA_SMP to the cap changed
nothing. With only 8 partitions one consumer has only 8 fetch streams, so this
For scale: this framework sustains 1.4M msgs/s at ~1 GB/s against a
200-partition topic on a 32-core staging host with CPU fully saturated. Raise
PARTITIONS if a future arm needs more headroom than the fan-out can buy.
The perthread figure (337,694) is deliberately NOT used as the denominator: no
arm runs four independent consumers, so it would be a ceiling nothing could
reach, which would make the headroom rule weaker rather than stricter.
